narrative:
The model predicts you have a 12% chance of failing your final year. While this is not a high probability, it is enough for the school to require you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The prediction that you might fail is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. The most influential factor is the reason you chose this school. Choosing it for its reputation, rather than for a specific course or other practical reasons, pushed the model toward expecting you to struggle. This is unusual, since students who passed were more likely to have chosen the school for its academic strengths in a particular subject.

The second most important factor is that you have had no past class failures. Surprisingly, this also nudged the prediction slightly toward failing. Among students who passed, having a completely clean record was actually the norm, so your zero failures did not provide the strong positive signal the model usually sees in successful students.

Third, the quality of your family relationships, which you described as good, worked in your favor and pulled the prediction back toward passing. Most students who succeed also report good or very good family support, so this is a helpful element in your profile.

To improve, focus on aligning your study habits more closely with the course content that matters most for final exams. Since you want to pursue higher education and already have family support, consider using that network to get targeted help in the subjects where your reputation-based school choice may have left gaps. Taking the remedial courses seriously will help close those gaps and raise your chances well above the current 12%.
